question: Trace Metal Coatings' dealings with its promoters and promoter-linked businesses across the FY2025 and FY2026 reports. What exposures existed, what changed, and are the disclosures consistent?
benchmark_answer:
# Trace Metal Coatings: Promoter and Promoter-Linked Dealings, FY2025 vs FY2026

**Scope:** The excerpts cover the FY2025 and FY2026 Annual Reports of Metal Coatings (India) Limited ("MCIL"). Citations are to "FY25 AR" and "FY26 AR" with page numbers. Several sections are truncated, so some conclusions below are provisional.

## 1. Exposures in FY2025

- **Khandelwal Busar Industries Pvt. Ltd. (KBIPL):** Mr. R.C. Khandelwal (WTD) and Mr. Pramod Khandelwal (MD) are directors with substantial interest. FY25 transactions were sales of ₹4,142.03 lakh, rent of ₹32.40 lakh and cash discount of ₹81.52 lakh [FY25 AR p29; p106]. Trade receivables from related parties were ₹153.51 lakh, down from ₹437.88 lakh in FY24 [FY25 AR p94; p106].
- **Loan to MD:** ₹560 lakh was given and ₹35 lakh repaid, leaving ₹525 lakh outstanding at 31 March 2025, repayable on demand. Interest received was ₹3.13 lakh [FY25 AR p107]. The CARO report classed this as loans to promoters and showed it as 98.50% of total loans in the nature of loans [FY25 AR p76].
- **Galva Strips Pvt. Ltd.:** A promoter entity (23.82% holding) with purchases of ₹86.95 lakh and ₹102.49 lakh payable at year-end [FY25 AR p106; p96].
- **Remuneration:** MD ₹263.67 lakh and WTD ₹270.17 lakh, each including ₹90 lakh bonus [FY25 AR p50; p106; p32].
- **Governance:** The RPT policy was amended on 14 February 2025 [FY25 AR p11]. The FY25 report states that no transactions were non-arm's length [FY25 AR p29].
- **Promoter holding:** 70.47% at 31 March 2025 [FY25 AR p96].

## 2. What changed in FY2026

| Item | FY2025 | FY2026 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| KBIPL sales | ₹4,142.03 lakh | ₹3,669.50 lakh | FY26 AR p31, p111; FY25 AR p106 |
| KBIPL receivable (year-end) | ₹153.51 lakh | ₹435.54 lakh | FY26 AR p99, p111 |
| KBIPL purchases / cash discount | Purchases nil; cash discount ₹81.52 lakh | Purchases ₹29.69 lakh; cash discount ₹70.72 lakh | FY26 AR p31, p111 |
| Loan to MD | ₹525 lakh outstanding | Nil; ₹100 lakh given, ₹625 lakh repaid | FY26 AR p112 |
| Loan to WTD | Nil | ₹26 lakh given; nil outstanding (the repayment row on p112 appears to continue from the previous page, so attribution is unclear) | FY26 AR p111–112 |
| MD remuneration | ₹263.67 lakh | ₹270.17 lakh (incl. ₹90 lakh bonus) | FY26 AR p33, p53 |
| Pramod Khandelwal HUF | Not shown | Commission on sales ₹9.00 lakh (Mr. Khandelwal is Karta) | FY26 AR p112 |
| Yash Khandelwal (son of MD) | Not shown | Joined 24.03.2026 as Chief Growth Officer; remuneration ₹39.19 lakh; ₹3.22 lakh payable | FY26 AR p33, p112 |
| Lehar Technologies.Com Pvt. Ltd. | Not in FY25 RPT table; MD listed as director | ₹2.00 lakh maintenance contract; entity now classed as promoter group (18,048 shares) | FY26 AR p111, p102; FY25 AR p132 |
| Promoter group holding | 70.47% | 70.94% | FY26 AR p102 |
| Promoter group additions | None | Lehar, Pushpa Gupta, Ajay Gupta (newly identified as promoter group) | FY26 AR p102 |

**Forward-looking approvals:**
- FY25 AR sought approval for KBIPL transactions up to ₹95 crore, from the 31st to the 32nd AGM [FY25 AR p128].
- FY26 AR seeks approval for the same ₹95 crore cap, from the 32nd to the 33rd AGM. The breakdown is sales ₹7,500 lakh, purchases ₹1,000 lakh, job work ₹500 lakh, rent ₹50 lakh and others ₹450 lakh [FY26 AR p139; p140].
- The proposed sales of ₹7,500 lakh are roughly double FY26 actual sales of ₹3,669.50 lakh.

**Other promoter-linked items:**
- Loans to firms in which directors are interested: "not granted," per FY26 AR p67. This statement covers entities, not loans to individual directors.
- Promoter shares are pledged or secured by personal guarantees of the WTD and MD for working-capital facilities [FY25 AR p97; FY26 AR p103].

## 3. Consistency of disclosures

**Consistent:**
- KBIPL FY25 figures agree across the AOC-2 form [FY25 AR p29] and Note 34 [FY25 AR p106].
- KBIPL FY26 figures agree across AOC-2 [FY26 AR p31] and Note 34 [FY26 AR p111].
- Prior-year comparatives agree between the FY25 and FY26 reports for the MD, WTD and CFO. Examples: MD ₹263.67 lakh; WTD ₹270.17 lakh; payables ₹52.14 lakh and ₹54.37 lakh [FY25 AR p106–107; FY26 AR p111–112].
- The promoter holdings reconcile to the reported totals in both years. I checked the sums: FY26 51,97,282 and FY25 51,63,590.
- The MD's loan movement reconciles: 525 + 100 − 625 = 0.

**Inconsistent or unclear:**
1. **Relative-employment statement.** FY26 AR p34 says "None of the above employees is the relative of any director." The same employee table includes Yash Khandelwal, the MD's son [FY26 AR p33, p112]. The statement's scope is unclear from the excerpt.
2. **Yash Khandelwal remuneration.** He commenced on 24.03.2026, yet ₹39.19 lakh is reported as FY26 remuneration. The excerpts do not explain this.
3. **Market-based pricing.** FY26 AR p139 states that pricing is "determined based on market competitiveness," and "No bidding process" was used. No valuation report was obtained [FY26 AR p139]. The arm's-length assertion therefore rests on internal representation.
4. **Certifier independence.** The Audit Committee relied on a certificate from the MD and CFO on the KBIPL transactions [FY26 AR p140]. The MD is an interested party.
5. **Turnover percentages.** FY26 AR p24 gives "around 64%" of turnover and "Not Available" for the related party's turnover. The same page gives related-party turnover of ₹7,028.27 lakh, so the "Not Available" entry is inconsistent with the table. The FY25 figure of "around 59%" [FY25 AR p129] equals KBIPL's FY25 sales divided by ₹7,028.27 lakh (4,142.03 / 7,028.27 = 58.9%). The FY26 "around 64%" approximates ₹45 crore (4,500 / 7,028.27 = 64.0%), not ₹95 crore. My arithmetic suggests the two percentages use different bases, but the excerpts do not state the basis. The p24 table is also truncated and does not name the related party.
6. **Loans to MD.** FY26 AR p82 states compliance with Sections 185 and 186. FY26 AR p67 discusses only loans to entities. The excerpts do not show how the ₹525 lakh loan to the MD, a director, was assessed under those provisions.
7. **Lehar classification.** Lehar was disclosed as an MD directorship in FY25 [FY25 AR p132] but was not a related party in the FY25 RPT table, and was added to the promoter group only in FY26. The reason for the change is not explained in the excerpts.
8. **Minor rounding.** FY25 AR p59 shows promoter holding as 70.48%, while the promoter table shows 70.47% for the same shares [FY25 AR p96]. The rounding is inconsistent.

## 4. Summary

The exposure to the MD's loan has closed, and the KBIPL receivable has risen back to roughly the FY24 level. Promoter holdings have increased, and the family's remuneration and related-party income have grown. The disclosures are largely consistent across the two reports in tables and comparatives. Key gaps remain: the relative-employment statement, the basis for turnover percentages, the valuation support for "arm's length" pricing, the independence of the certifier, and the compliance treatment of the director loan.

question: Looking at Metal Coatings' FY2026 balance sheet against FY2025, is liquidity getting tighter? Explain where cash has been absorbed and how it was funded.
benchmark_answer:
## Short answer

Liquidity is tighter in substance. Operating cash flow turned negative, the company borrowed more, and adjusted net debt rose. The headline current ratio is still strong, though it slipped slightly.

## Headline liquidity measures

- **Current ratio** fell to 4.49x from 4.73x, a 5.13% decline [Metal Coatings_Annual Report FY 2026.pdf, p38; p110].
- **Current assets** rose to ₹5,000.95 lakhs from ₹4,622.65 lakhs. **Current liabilities** rose to ₹1,114.04 lakhs from ₹976.93 lakhs [FY 2026 p88].
- **Adjusted net debt** rose to ₹327.82 lakhs from ₹137.91 lakhs [FY 2026 p110].
- **Cash and cash equivalents** were ₹10.85 lakhs, up from ₹8.56 lakhs [FY 2026 p88; p101]. Other bank balances fell to ₹17.56 lakhs from ₹20.24 lakhs [FY 2026 p101].

## Where cash was absorbed

- **Operating cash flow turned negative.** Net cash used in operating activities was ₹115.84 lakhs, compared with ₹569.06 lakhs generated in the prior year [FY 2026 p90].
- **Trade receivables increased by ₹674.56 lakhs**, to ₹2,905.90 lakhs from ₹2,231.34 lakhs. This was a cash outflow in FY2026 after a ₹624.42 lakh inflow in FY2025 [FY 2026 p88, p89, p90].
- **Inventories increased by ₹213.60 lakhs**, to ₹1,050.27 lakhs from ₹836.67 lakhs. Work in progress rose most, to ₹351.62 lakhs from ₹178.63 lakhs [FY 2026 p88, p99].
- **Operating profit was thin.** Operating profit before working capital changes was ₹272.59 lakhs, and cash generated from operations was negative at ₹(24.51) lakhs [FY 2026 p90].
- **Investments** increased to ₹923.62 lakhs from ₹821.45 lakhs. The cash flow shows net purchases of mutual funds of ₹30.54 lakhs (₹3,135.00 purchased less ₹3,104.46 sold) [FY 2026 p90; p99].

## How it was funded

- **Borrowings rose sharply.** Borrowings increased to ₹352.11 lakhs from ₹159.64 lakhs, and the cash flow shows ₹192.47 lakhs of new overdraft borrowings [FY 2026 p88, p90, p103].
- **Other assets released cash.** Loans to employees fell to ₹9.47 lakhs from ₹532.98 lakhs, and other current assets fell to ₹49.14 lakhs from ₹142.39 lakhs. The cash flow shows a ₹615.32 lakh inflow from other assets [FY 2026 p88, p90, p101]. This was a one-off source of cash rather than recurring cash generation.
- **Lower interest cost helped.** Finance costs fell to ₹1.41 lakhs from ₹237.41 lakhs [FY 2026 p89], which reduced financing outflows.
- **Dividend outflow.** A dividend of ₹73.27 lakhs was paid in FY2026 [FY 2026 p90].
- **Net result.** Net cash flow for the year was ₹2.29 lakhs, against ₹0.61 lakhs in FY2025 [FY 2026 p90].

## Caveats

- Working capital (current assets less current liabilities) rose to about ₹3,886.91 lakhs from about ₹3,645.72 lakhs. The excerpts do not provide a quick ratio, so I cannot assess liquidity excluding inventories.
- The excerpts do not state the terms or maturity of the overdraft facility beyond its security arrangements [FY 2026 p103].
- Trade payables fell to ₹107.90 lakhs from ₹148.30 lakhs [FY 2026 p103], which reduced supplier financing.

question: If you had to re-underwrite Metal Coatings today using both of its last two annual reports, would your view of its creditworthiness change? Weigh the external rating, audit outcomes, earnings trend, related-party reliance and balance-sheet strength.
benchmark_answer:
## Short answer

On the documents provided, the external rating and audit signals are unchanged, but the FY2026 cash flow and working-capital picture is weaker than FY2025. Leverage is still low but rising, and reliance on one related party has grown. I would not upgrade the view. Whether it changes materially depends on how much weight you give the operating cash outflow. The excerpts cannot show whether that outflow is temporary.

## 1. External rating

- **Unchanged.** Acuité reaffirmed 'ACUITE BBB' (long-term) and 'ACUITE A3+' (short-term) on January 22, 2026, with outlook 'Stable' [Metal Coatings_Annual Report FY 2026, p10]. The same ratings and outlook appear in the FY2025 report [FY 2025, p61].
- The excerpts do not contain the rating rationale or any later rating action.

## 2. Audit outcomes and governance

- **FY2026:** unmodified opinion on the financial statements [FY 2026, p70]; adequate internal financial controls over Ind AS reporting [FY 2026, p87]; no fraud reported under Section 143(12) [FY 2026, p24]; no material internal audit observations [FY 2026, p13].
- **FY2025:** no qualification in the auditor's report [FY 2025, p63]. The auditor found nothing indicating a material uncertainty about meeting liabilities falling due within one year, while stating this is not an assurance of future viability [FY 2025, p79].
- **Auditor change:** Mehra Goel & Co. has converted to an LLP (letter dated June 23, 2026). The board proposes re-appointing the firm for five years at a fee of Rs 9 lakh [FY 2026, p10, p135]. This is a continuity point, not an adverse finding.
- No insolvency proceedings were pending at March 31, 2026 [FY 2026, p24], and the company reports no default on loans or interest [FY 2026, p10, p83].

## 3. Earnings trend (Rs lakhs)

| Metric | FY24 | FY25 | FY26 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue from operations | 16,841.44 | 16,025.02 | 14,897.55 | FY25 p5; FY26 p6 |
| Profit before tax | 319.74 | 307.78 | 318.69 | FY25 p5; FY26 p6 |
| Profit after tax | 249.83 | 236.96 | 239.97 | FY25 p5; FY26 p6 |
| Finance cost | 0.93 | 237.41 | 1.41 | FY25 p5; FY26 p6 |
| EBITDA margin (%) | 2.22 | 3.78 | 2.53 | FY25 p37; FY26 p39 |
| ROCE (%) | 8.30 | 13.03 | 7.18 | FY25 p37; FY26 p39 |

- Revenue has fallen for two consecutive years, down about 11.6% from FY24 to FY26 (my calculation).
- Profit is flat, held up by lower finance costs. The FY25 spike was attributed to a one-time interest payment to HSIIDC [FY 2025, p37].
- Operating margin fell back in FY26, and the company attributes the ROCE fall to lower pre-interest earnings [FY 2026, p39].

## 4. Related-party reliance

- **Concentration:** sales to Khandelwal Busar Industries Pvt. Ltd. (KBIPL), in which the MD and WTD have substantial interest, were Rs 3,669.50 lakhs in FY26 versus Rs 4,142.03 lakhs in FY25 [FY 2026, p111; FY 2025, p106]. By my calculation, that is about 25% of FY26 revenue and about 26% of FY25 revenue.
- **Receivables:** dues from related parties rose to Rs 435.54 lakhs from Rs 153.51 lakhs [FY 2026, p99]. That is about 15% of trade receivables (my calculation).
- **Forward approvals:** the board seeks omnibus approval for KBIPL transactions of about Rs 45 crore to FY27 and Rs 50 crore thereafter [FY 2026, p139].
- **Loans to promoter:** the MD's loan balance was Rs 525 lakhs at FY25 year-end [FY 2025, p107]. In FY26, Rs 625 lakhs was repaid and Rs 100 lakhs given. Total loans fell to Rs 9.47 lakhs [FY 2026, p88, p112].
- **Guarantees:** bank working-capital facilities are secured by hypothecation and by personal guarantees from the WTD and MD [FY 2026, p103].
- The company states all related-party transactions were at arm's length [FY 2026, p14].

## 5. Balance-sheet strength and liquidity

- **Leverage (positive but worsening):** borrowings rose to Rs 352.11 lakhs from Rs 159.64 lakhs. Debt-equity moved to 0.08 from 0.04 [FY 2026, p38, p88]. Adjusted net debt rose to Rs 327.82 lakhs from Rs 137.91 lakhs [FY 2026, p110]. Equity rose to Rs 4,397.00 lakhs [FY 2026, p88].
- **Cash flow (negative):** net cash used in operating activities was Rs (115.84) lakhs versus Rs 569.06 lakhs in FY25. The drivers were a Rs (674.56) lakh increase in trade receivables and a Rs (213.60) lakh increase in inventories [FY 2026, p90].
- **Working capital:** trade receivables rose to Rs 2,905.90 lakhs from Rs 2,231.34 lakhs, with no allowance for doubtful debts [FY 2026, p88, p99]. Inventory turnover fell to 14.29 from 19.53 [FY 2026, p38].
- **Liquidity ratios:** current ratio eased to 4.49 from 4.73, still strong [FY 2026, p38]. Cash and cash equivalents were only Rs 10.85 lakhs [FY 2026, p88].
- Contingent tax disputes are small (about Rs 2.45 lakhs in total) [FY 2026, p112].

## Conclusion

- **Unchanged:** the BBB/A3+ rating and Stable outlook; the clean audit opinion; no defaults or insolvency; small contingent liabilities.
- **Weaker:** operating cash flow turned negative; receivables and inventory grew while revenue fell; EBITDA margin and ROCE declined; sales to one promoter-linked party remain about a quarter of revenue, with higher receivables from it.
- **Still supportive:** low absolute debt and a strong current ratio.

Based only on these excerpts, I would hold a cautious view rather than a clearly changed one. The main question for re-underwriting is whether the FY26 working-capital build reverses. The excerpts do not show any post-year-end cash position, receivable collection, or rating rationale.

The Company reported revenue from operations of ₹16,025.02 lakhs as compared to ₹16,841.44 lakhs in the previous financial year. This decline reflects the broader challenges faced by the steel industry during the year, including intensified competition, fluctuations in global steel prices, and a slowdown in demand across key domestic and international markets.

Further, the Company reported a net profit of ₹236.96 lakhs for the financial year ended March 31, 2025, as against ₹249.83 lakhs in the previous financial year, reflecting a marginal decline. The decrease in profitability was primarily attributable to an increase in finance costs, which exerted downward pressure on the bottom line. Looking forward, the Company is actively exploring strategic initiatives aimed at enhancing financial performance. Key focus areas include improving working capital efficiency, optimizing cost structures, and implementing targeted operational efficiencies. These measures are expected to support profitability and strengthen the Company's financial resilience in the coming years. The management remains cautiously optimistic about the future prospects and is committed to navigating through these challenging times with resilience and adaptability.

question: Bhadora Industries listed on the SME platform after a year of rapid growth. From a lender's perspective, how is that growth being financed and what do the quality of its receivables and working capital look like?
benchmark_answer:
# Bhadora Industries: Growth Financing, Receivables and Working Capital (Lender View)

*"Annual Report" refers to Bhadora Industries_Annual Report.pdf. All figures are FY2024-25 unless stated; amounts are in lakhs.*

## 1. Scale of growth

- Revenue from operations rose to 11,011.18 from 8,139.32 [Annual Report p71; p76].
- Profit before tax rose to 1,385.51 from 676.65 [Annual Report p19].
- Profit after tax rose to 1,014.93 from 501.79 [Annual Report p19].
- The Board did not recommend a dividend, to "strengthen the financial resources" of the company [Annual Report p20].

## 2. How the growth is financed

**Operating cash flow was thin relative to growth.** Net cash from operating activities was 351.68 (prior year 271.58), after a 957.75 cash outflow for trade receivables [Annual Report p72].

**Capex and receivables were funded mainly with debt.**
- Net cash used in investing was (845.17), including (729.95) for acquisition of fixed assets [Annual Report p72].
- Financing inflow was 741.85, comprising long-term borrowings of 366.22 and short-term borrowing proceeds of 653.39 [Annual Report p72].

**Borrowings have risen sharply.**
- Current borrowings (bank loans, other secured loans and current maturities) were 1,483.29, up from 829.89 [Annual Report p74].
- Term loans were 483.35, up from 117.13. The main addition is a SIDBI loan of 440.50 (prior year nil) [Annual Report p74].
- The SIDBI loan funds equipment purchases of Rs 539 lakhs, repayable in 66 installments of Rs 8.20 lakhs [Annual Report p74].

**Working capital lines and security:**
- ICICI Bank cash credit limit of 1,000 lakhs at 9.00%, secured by hypothecation of stock, assignment of debtors and personal property of directors [Annual Report p74].
- Indian Bank overdraft of 200 lakhs at 9.75%, pari passu with ICICI over current assets, with 30 lakhs of FDRs as collateral [Annual Report p74].
- Yes Bank working capital demand loan at 10.25% [Annual Report p75], and a Yes Bank letter of credit facility [Annual Report p74].
- Bank loans from banks (secured) were 1,170.88, up from 630.30. This exceeds the ICICI limit alone, so other limits are also in use. The excerpts do not give utilisation by facility.

**Other funding points:**
- Unsecured loans from directors and relatives (82.72 and 28.29 in the prior year) are now nil. They were on oral terms, interest-free [Annual Report p74].
- The company created or modified charges on its assets during the year [Annual Report p36].
- The IPO (54,00,000 shares at INR 103, issue size INR 5,562 lakhs) was approved and listed on NSE Emerge on 11 August 2025, after year-end [Annual Report p21; p34]. The auditor states the company raised no money through an IPO during the year [Annual Report p65]. FY25 growth was therefore not funded by IPO proceeds.
- A bonus issue of 1,15,50,000 shares (31 December 2024) was capitalised from accumulated surplus, which fell from 903.80 to 463.73 [Annual Report p21; p73]. This is non-cash.

**Leverage and coverage:**

| Ratio | FY25 | FY24 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Debt-equity | 0.94 | 0.89 | Annual Report p41 |
| Current ratio | 1.59 | 1.55 | Annual Report p41 |
| DSCR (PBITD / finance costs) | 6.68 | 5.06 | Annual Report p81 |
| Return on capital employed | 0.40 | 0.42 | Annual Report p42 |

Finance costs rose to 277.77 from 203.20 [Annual Report p77].

The auditor reports no default on loans and borrowings [Annual Report p65], no cash losses [Annual Report p66], and no material uncertainty about meeting liabilities due within one year [Annual Report p66].

## 3. Quality of receivables

**Receivables have grown faster than sales.**
- Trade receivables rose to 2,177.41 from 1,219.65, up about 78.5% [Annual Report p76]. Revenue grew about 35%.
- Trade receivable turnover fell to 1.62 from 9.68, a 83.26% decline. The company attributes this to higher receivables [Annual Report p41; p81].
- Net capital turnover fell to 8.11 from 9.07, due to an increase in sundry debtors [Annual Report p81].

**Ageing (as at 31 March 2025) [Annual Report p76]:**

| Category | <6 months | 6m–1 yr | 1–2 yrs | 2–3 yrs | >3 yrs | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Undisputed | 953.51 | 132.58 | 0.20 | 0.76 | 8.79 | 1,095.83 |
| Disputed | 50.64 | 73.18 | – | – | – | 123.82 |

- Of the schedule's 1,219.65 total, about 82% is under six months. About 215.5 (17.7%) is over six months, including 73.18 of disputed amounts.
- The disputed balance is 123.82 (about 10% of the schedule total).
- **Reconciliation gap:** the ageing total of 1,219.65 matches the prior-year receivables figure, not the current 2,177.41 in Note 15. A reconciled ageing should be requested before relying on it.

**Reconciliation of debtors to bank statements [Annual Report p81]:**
- Q4 variance of 42.86 (statement 2,137.73 vs books 2,180.59). The explanation is that the auditor moved a creditor into the debtors list.
- Q1 variance of (2.70) was due to a TDS mismatch.

**Concentration and contract risk:** the company has no long-term customer contracts, and government business is won through bidding [Annual Report p39].

## 4. Working capital

**Inventory**
- Inventories rose to 981.42 from 829.20 [Annual Report p76].
- Inventory turnover improved to 12.16 from 9.13 [Annual Report p41].

**Payables**
- Total trade payables fell to 416.41 from 466.98 [Annual Report p75].
- MSME payables rose to 384.85 from 312.55, now about 92% of trade payables [Annual Report p75].
- Payable turnover rose to 19.21 from 14.80. The company says this reflects faster payments to suppliers or reduced credit availed [Annual Report p41].

**Other current liabilities**
- Total rose to 148.03 from 89.71, mainly GST payable (48.07 vs 9.06) [Annual Report p75].

**Cash**
- Cash and bank balances rose to 276.50 from 28.14 [Annual Report p76]. This comes mainly from borrowings.

**Stock statements submitted to banks versus books [Annual Report p80; p64]:**
- Quarterly variances were 246.06, 307.58, nil and 65.81. The company cites timing differences and clerical or rounding errors.
- ICICI statement variances were 243.36, 307.58, (0.03) and 108.67 across June 2024 to March 2025. The March 2025 explanation includes that the auditor changed a creditor to a debtor.
- Lenders should treat these as a control weakness, since the lending base depends on these statements.

## 5. Gaps and inconsistencies

- Return on Net Worth is shown as 64.39 [Annual Report p42], while Return on Equity is shown as 0.49 [Annual Report p81]. These measures are not reconciled in the excerpts.
- The IPO describes total capital of 5,562 lakhs from 54,00,000 shares, while the balance sheet shows share capital of 1,320 lakhs from 1,32,00,000 shares at 31 March 2025 [Annual Report p34; p73]. The excerpts do not explain the difference.
- The excerpts do not show sanctioned versus drawn limits, debtor concentration by customer, or the use of IPO proceeds.

## Summary for the lender

Growth has been funded largely by bank and term debt, with receivables absorbing a large share of working capital. Profitability and inventory turns have improved, and the auditor reports no default. However, receivables have grown much faster than sales, part of the ageing is disputed, the ageing schedule does not reconcile to the balance sheet, and stock and debtor statements to banks have recurring variances. A lender would likely require reconciled ageing, a month-by-month borrowing base check, and an explanation of the MSME payables increase before relying on the current limits.

question: How reliable is the financial information Bhadora Industries gives its lenders and shareholders? Look for internal inconsistencies across the directors' report, auditor annexures and the notes.
benchmark_answer:
# Reliability of Bhadora Industries' Financial Information

**Short answer:** The headline numbers are internally consistent, but the supporting disclosures are not. Revenue, profit and balance-sheet totals tie across the report, notes and statements. However, the ratio table, EPS, shareholding, related-party, property and bank-return disclosures contain errors or contradictions that a lender or shareholder could not rely on without verification.

In this answer, "AR" means *Bhadora Industries_Annual Report.pdf*. Calculations are mine, derived from figures in the excerpts.

## 1. What ties out

- **Revenue ₹11,011.18 lakh** appears consistently in the chairman's letter [AR p5], directors' report [AR p19], segment note [AR p40] and Note 19 [AR p71, p77].
- **Profit after tax ₹1,014.93 lakh** matches across [AR p5, p19, p20, p71]. Tax reconciles: PBT 1,385.51 − current tax 360.59 − deferred tax 10.00 = 1,014.92 (rounding) [AR p71].
- **Balance sheet** totals ₹4,876.16 lakh (FY25) and ₹2,586.67 lakh (FY24) on both sides [AR p70]. Notes 13–18 sum to their balance-sheet lines.
- **FY25 cash flow** reconciles to the balance-sheet cash movement (28.14 → 276.50) [AR p72].
- **Current ratio (1.59), debt-equity (0.94) and inventory turnover (12.16)** recompute from the balance sheet.
- **CSR** arithmetic is correct: 2% of ₹2,39,45,458.50 = ₹4,78,909.17; spend of ₹5,00,000 gives an excess of ₹21,090.83 [AR p53–56].

## 2. Material inconsistencies

**a) Cash flow, FY24 financing section [AR p72]**
The components sum to −67.76 (−65.58 + 201.02 − 203.20), but the reported subtotal is −268.78. The reported net change (−133.30) only works with the subtotal. The FY24 financing section therefore does not add up.

**b) Earnings per share and share count [AR p19, p71, p81 vs p82]**
- FY24 EPS is reported as ₹30.41 [AR p19, p71, p81], which uses 16.5 lakh pre-bonus shares.
- The EPS note shows FY24 basic EPS of ₹3.80 and weighted shares of 132.00 lakh for both years [AR p82]. ₹501.79 lakh ÷ 132 lakh = ₹3.80.
- The bonus issue of 1,15,50,000 shares [AR p21] is therefore not reflected consistently in the prior-year EPS.

**c) Return on net worth [AR p42 vs p81]**
Return on Net Worth is shown as 64.39% (FY25) and 61.35% (FY24) [AR p42]. The Return on Equity ratio in the notes is 0.49 and 0.47 [AR p81]. My calculation (PAT ÷ total equity 2,083.73) gives 0.49, so the 64.39% figure does not match.

**d) Ratio table versus balance sheet [AR p41, p81]**
- *Trade receivables turnover 1.62 (FY25):* Sales ₹11,011.18 lakh ÷ average receivables ((1,219.65 + 2,177.41)/2 = 1,698.5) ≈ 6.5. The stated 1.62 cannot be reproduced. The FY24 figure of 9.68 does reproduce.
- *Net capital turnover 8.11 (FY25) and 9.07 (FY24):* Working capital from the balance sheet is 1,318.2 (FY25) and 763.4 (FY24), giving about 8.35 and 10.66.
- *Return on capital employed 0.40 (FY25):* EBIT 1,663.3 ÷ (equity 2,083.7 + LT debt 483.4) ≈ 0.65.
- *Debt service coverage 6.68 (FY25):* PBITD 1,697.3 ÷ finance cost 277.8 ≈ 6.11.
- Minor: inventory and payables turnover % changes differ slightly from the ratios shown (33.19% vs 33.21%; 29.80% vs 29.73%).

**e) "Net profit before tax & depreciation" [AR p41]**
The narrative says "Net profit before tax & depreciation is Rs. 1,385.51 Lacs as against Rs. 501.79 Lacs." This is wrong on both counts: 1,385.51 is PBT (not before depreciation), and 501.79 is the prior-year PAT, not PBT (676.65).

**f) Property, plant and equipment, FY24 [AR p70, p85 vs p75]**
FY24 PPE is ₹184.57 lakh on the balance sheet and in the depreciation schedule, but ₹204.36 lakh in the PPE table [AR p75].

**g) Immovable property [AR p63 vs p80, p76]**
The auditor states the company owns no immovable property and that the building sits on rented land [AR p63]. Yet the related-party note records payments "against purchase of Land" and "purchase of Property" of ₹26.00 lakh [AR p80], and Note 17 carries an advance of ₹26.00 lakh "for purchase of property" [AR p76].

**h) Ind AS basis [AR p23 vs p42]**
The directors' report says the company is exempt from Ind AS because it is listed on an SME platform [AR p23]. Another section says the statements are prepared under Ind AS [AR p42]. The listing is dated 11 August 2025 [AR p21], after the 31 March 2025 reporting date, so the exemption rationale does not clearly apply to these statements.

**i) Remuneration disclosure [AR p50 vs p80]**
- The directors' report shows a 84.62% increase for Anil and Pradeep Bhadora [AR p50]. The related-party note shows remuneration rising from ₹13.00 lakh to ₹22.50 lakh, a 73.08% increase [AR p80].
- Shashank Bhadora is shown as "Nil" change [AR p50], but his remuneration went from 0.00 to 22.50 [AR p80].

**j) Shareholding [AR p73]**
- Shashank Bhadora held 0 shares at 31 March 2024 but 24,30,560 shares (18.41%) at 31 March 2025, with a "% change" of 18.41. The bonus issue cannot explain a holding that started at zero.
- The bonus ratio implied by [AR p21] and [AR p73] is 7:1 (11,550,000 bonus on 1,650,000). On that basis, Pradeep's 874,500 shares should be about 6,996,000 and Anil's 775,500 about 6,204,000. The reported 6,126,560 and 3,486,560 do not reconcile.

**k) Bank quarterly returns versus books [AR p64, p80, p81]**
- The ICICI March 2025 variance is shown as 108.67, but 3,162.01 − 3,053.54 = 108.47.
- Q1 (June 2024) stock variance is 243.36 in the bank table [AR p64] but 246.06 in the stock table [AR p80]. The two tables use different bases.
- The Q4 debtors "per books" figure is 2,180.59 [AR p81], but Note 15 shows 2,177.41 [AR p76].
- Variances are attributed to timing, clerical errors and rounding. One Q4 reason states: "Auditer change one creditors to debtors list" [AR p64, p81]. That is an auditor-driven reclassification affecting what was reported to banks.
- Q4 stock variance is 65.81 but 915.60 vs 981.42 gives 65.82 [AR p80].

**l) Corporate and shareholder labels**
- The CIN still carries a private-company code ("PTC") on the statements after conversion to a public limited company [AR p70, p34].
- The FY25 share capital is described as "issued for cash" [AR p73], but 1,155 lakh of it is bonus shares [AR p21, p73].

**m) Director loans [AR p74, p80]**
Loans from directors and relatives of ₹110.67 lakh at FY24 (Pradeep 82.72, Shashank 5.90, Sandhya 22.05) are shown as nil at FY25. The excerpts do not show where these balances appear on the balance sheet or how they were repaid.

**n) Audit fee [AR p78, p77]**
The FY25 audit fee includes ₹6.00 lakh for a prior period. Audit and certification expense rises from ₹2.00 lakh to ₹25.40 lakh [AR p77].

## 3. Assurance statements that conflict with the data

- The directors state that auditor notes are "self-explanatory" and need no comment [AR p29].
- The auditor says internal financial controls operated effectively [AR p69], and the internal-control section asserts adequate controls [AR p42]. Yet the bank returns show multiple unexplained variances and a creditor-to-debtor reclassification [AR p64, p80, p81].
- The auditor reports no material uncertainty about meeting liabilities [AR p66], but the bank returns were not in agreement with the books for most quarters [AR p80].

## 4. Gaps the excerpts cannot close

- No subsequent-events note is included, so the IPO (54,00,000 shares at ₹103, aggregate ₹5,562 lakh) [AR p21] cannot be checked against the statements. The balance sheet shows 132 lakh shares.
- The CSR average net profit of ₹239.45 lakh [AR p53] implies a FY23 figure that is not in the excerpts.
- The IPO expenses of ₹38.24 lakh sit in other non-current assets [AR p76]. The excerpts do not explain this treatment.

## 5. Implications

- **For lenders:** The bank-return variances (up to ₹307.58 lakh in September 2024) and the debtor and stock mismatches are the most direct concern. Ratios used in lending decisions (receivables turnover, return on capital, coverage) cannot be reproduced from the balance sheet.
- **For shareholders:** EPS for the comparative year, promoter holdings and remuneration disclosures are inconsistent. The basis of accounting is contradictory.
- **Overall:** Verify the FY24 financing cash flow, prior-year EPS, promoter share register, bank-return reconciliations and the Ind AS basis against the audited ledgers before relying on the ratios or shareholder data.

question: GRM Overseas' sales fell this year but its receivables did not. How worried should a lender be about collections and liquidity, and does the company's own credit-loss accounting reflect the risk?
benchmark_answer:
**Bottom line:** A lender should be moderately worried, not alarmed. Receivables stayed flat while standalone sales fell about 23%, so the receivable base is now large relative to sales. Ageing has also shifted toward older balances, and the company's own accounts show no credit-loss allowance or impairment, which is hard to reconcile with that ageing. Liquidity ratios improved, but largely through borrowing reduction and an equity-type inflow. The excerpts do not show the allowance balance or the bad-debt charge, so the credit-loss question cannot be fully answered.

*Source key: "GRM AR" = GRM Overseas Annual Report FY 2025.pdf. The ASC 326 and CECL handbook excerpts are US GAAP material and are not the company's framework (the auditor refers to Ind AS statements [GRM AR p129]). I use them only to describe general principles, not to judge compliance.*

**1. Sales vs. receivables**
- Standalone revenue fell to Rs 91,314.68 lakhs from Rs 1,18,582.93 lakhs [GRM AR p19; p135].
- Standalone trade receivables were Rs 46,551.12 lakhs versus Rs 46,668.93 lakhs, essentially flat [GRM AR p133].
- Consolidated revenue rose to Rs 1,34,819.28 lakhs from Rs 1,31,244.18 lakhs, and consolidated receivables were Rs 48,005.45 lakhs versus Rs 48,188.09 lakhs [GRM AR p19; p205].
- Export revenue fell from 1,016.3 to 256.6 and Foodkraft from 782.9 to 538.5 (units as labelled in the chart) [GRM AR p17].
- Trade receivable turnover fell to 1.96x from 2.74x (standalone). The company attributes this to "extended credit period allowed to customers" [GRM AR p169]. This is the clearest signal of collection stress.

**2. Ageing (standalone, 31 March 2025)** [GRM AR p150]
- Under 6 months: Rs 24,484.48 lakhs (about 53%)
- 6 months to 1 year: Rs 17,831.44 lakhs (about 38%)
- 1 to 2 years: Rs 4,235.22 lakhs (about 9%)
- Credit-impaired and "significant increase in credit risk" buckets: nil.

The percentages are my calculation from these figures. The standalone FY24 ageing is not in the excerpts. The consolidated ageing table [GRM AR p206] shows Rs 767.13 lakhs at 2–3 years and Rs 203.14 lakhs at 1–2 years for the prior-year balance, so the older tail is not new, but the 1–2 year bucket is much larger in the FY25 standalone figures.

**3. Concentration and related parties**
- GRM International Holdings (UK) owes Rs 1,549.39 lakhs, up from Rs 1,363.44 lakhs. GRM Foodkraft's Rs 883.10 lakhs balance from FY24 is nil in FY25 [GRM AR p150].
- Trade receivables of the holding company are hypothecated to SBI, PNB and Union Bank against working capital limits [GRM AR p205]. This means receivables are pledged to lenders and are not free collateral for a new lender.

**4. Liquidity**
- Current ratio: 1.80x versus 1.66x (consolidated) [GRM AR p17; p225]. Standalone: 1.73x versus 1.63x [GRM AR p169].
- Gross debt/equity fell to 0.85x from 1.18x (consolidated) [GRM AR p17; p225]. Standalone was 0.93x from 1.28x [GRM AR p169].
- Standalone cash rose to Rs 3,248.86 lakhs from Rs 458.85 lakhs [GRM AR p133].
- Standalone operating cash flow was Rs 5,597.72 lakhs versus Rs 3,616.18 lakhs. Short-term borrowings were repaid, and the company reports Rs 3,401.26 lakhs of money received against share warrants [GRM AR p137].
- Inventory rose to Rs 30,271.06 lakhs from Rs 21,194.05 lakhs, and inventory days rose to 102 from 60 [GRM AR p133; p17]. Inventory build is a larger liquidity drain than receivables here.
- Other current liabilities jumped to Rs 7,691.68 lakhs from Rs 358.25 lakhs [GRM AR p133]. The excerpts do not explain this.
- Export credit facilities and working capital limits are repayable on demand [GRM AR p158]. Working capital limits from banks were Rs 26,921.37 lakhs [GRM AR p157].
- The auditor reports no default on loans, no wilful default, and no material uncertainty about meeting liabilities due within one year [GRM AR p127; p129]. The auditor's report is unqualified [GRM AR p26].

**5. Does the credit-loss accounting reflect the risk?**
- The stated policy is the simplified approach, with lifetime expected losses recognised from initial recognition for trade receivables [GRM AR p146; p201].
- The consolidated note defines default as receivables past due by one year [GRM AR p221]. The standalone 1–2 year bucket of Rs 4,235.22 lakhs [GRM AR p150] would therefore appear to meet that definition, yet it is classed as "undisputed – considered good" with no credit-impaired amount. The excerpts give no explanation, so this is a point to challenge.
- No allowance balance, expected-credit-loss provision or bad-debt expense line appears in the excerpts. Other expenses rose to Rs 12,235.95 lakhs from Rs 9,657.57 lakhs [GRM AR p135], but no breakdown is given.
- The company's general description of credit risk monitoring refers to internal credit limits [GRM AR p221], but the excerpts contain no quantitative credit-limit or collection data.

**What a lender should request**
- The standalone and consolidated expected-credit-loss allowance and its movement for FY25 and FY24.
- The standalone ageing for FY24, and an explanation of the Rs 4,235 lakh 1–2 year bucket.
- Details of the extended credit terms granted to customers, and whether the UK related-party receivable is collectible and on what terms.
- An explanation of the jump in other current liabilities.
- The status of export incentives receivable, which fell to Rs 451.98 lakhs from Rs 806.54 lakhs [GRM AR p151].

Analysis: column chart — Inventory Days increased significantly from 60 in FY24 to 102 in FY25, a 70% increase, suggesting higher inventory build-up. FY24 bar in light grey (#C8C8C8), FY25 bar in gold (#F5C518).

Description: A two-bar column chart comparing Gross Debt/Equity ratio for FY24 and FY25.

Description: A two-bar column chart comparing Current Ratio for FY24 and FY25.
Analysis: column chart — Current Ratio improved from 1.66x in FY24 to 1.80x in FY25, reflecting improved short-term liquidity. FY24 bar in light grey (#C8C8C8), FY25 bar in gold (#F5C518).

Description: A two-bar column chart comparing Interest Coverage Ratio for FY24 and FY25.
Analysis: column chart — Interest Coverage Ratio improved from 5.08x in FY24 to 5.95x in FY25, indicating stronger debt servicing capacity. FY24 bar in light grey (#C8C8C8), FY25 bar in gold (#F5C518).

Description: A combination column and line chart showing EBITDA in Rs. Cr. (bars) and EBITDA margin % (line/labels above) for FY22 through FY25. FY25 bar highlighted in gold.

Revenue is measured based on transaction price, which is the fair value of the consideration received or receivable, stated net of discounts, returns and Indirect Taxes. A) Credit risk

Credit risk is the risk of financial loss to the Company if a customer or counterparty to a financial instrument fails to meet its contractual obligations, and arises principally from the Company's receivables from customers and investments in debt securities. The carrying amount of financial assets represents the maximum credit exposure.

The Company assesses and manages credit risk based on internal credit rating system, continuously monitoring defaults of customers and other counterparties, identified either individually or by the company, and incorporates this information into its credit risk controls. Internal credit rating is performed for each class of financial instruments with different characteristics. The Company assigns the following credit ratings to each class of financial assets based on the assumptions, inputs and factors specific to the class of financial assets.

Credit risk is the risk of financial loss to the Group if a customer or counterparty to a financial instrument fails to meet its contractual obligations, and arises principally from the Group's receivables from customers and investments in debt securities. The carrying amount of financial assets represents the maximum credit exposure.
Trade receivables

The Group closely monitors the credit-worthiness of the debtors through internal systems that are configured to define credit limits of customers, thereby, limiting the credit risk to pre-calculated amounts. The Group assesses increase in credit risk on an ongoing basis for amounts receivable that become past due and default is considered to have occurred when amounts receivable become past due one year.

FASB ASC 326 Update.pdf.section_name: > Developing an Estimate of Expected Credit Losses
FASB ASC 326 Update.pdf.content:
326-20-30-7 When developing an estimate of expected credit losses on financial asset(s), an entity shall consider available information relevant to assessing the collectibility of cash flows. This information may include internal information, external information, or a combination of both relating to past events, current conditions, and reasonable and supportable forecasts. An entity shall consider relevant qualitative and quantitative factors that relate to the environment in which the entity operates and are specific to the borrower(s). When financial assets are evaluated on a collective or individual basis, an entity is not required to search all possible information that is not reasonably available without undue cost and effort. Furthermore, an entity is not required to develop a hypothetical pool of financial assets. An entity may find that using its internal information is sufficient in determining collectibility.

326-20-30-8 Historical credit loss experience of financial assets with similar risk characteristics generally provides a basis for an entity's assessment of expected credit losses. Historical loss information can be internal or external

Why Is the FASB Issuing This Accounting Standards Update (Update)?

The Board is issuing this Update to address challenges encountered when applying the guidance in Topic 326, Financial Instruments—Credit Losses, to current accounts receivable and current contract assets arising from transactions accounted for under Topic 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers. The Private Company Council (PCC) initiated this project in response to concerns raised by private company stakeholders.

Stakeholders indicated that identifying, analyzing, and documenting macroeconomic data (such as unemployment rates and property values, among others) as part of developing reasonable and supportable forecasts when estimating expected credit losses for these balances under Subtopic 326-20, Financial Instruments—Credit Losses—Measured at Amortized Cost, can be costly and complex and generally does not have a material effect on the estimate of expected credit losses for short-term assets.

In addition, stakeholders observed that estimating expected credit losses for current accounts receivable and current contract assets that were collected before the date that the financial statements were available to be issued can require significant effort and documentation and can result in recording expected credit losses for amounts that have been subsequently collected. As such, stakeholders noted that the ability to consider collection activity after the balance sheet date when estimating expected credit losses would provide investors and other financial statement users with decision-useful information while significantly reducing complexity for preparers.

To address this feedback, the amendments in this Update introduce a practical expedient for all entities and an accounting policy election for entities other than public business entities related to applying Subtopic 326-20 to current accounts receivable and current contract assets arising from transactions accounted for under Topic 606.

The amendments in this Update provide (1) all entities with a practical expedient and (2) entities other than public business entities with an accounting policy election when estimating expected credit losses for current accounts receivable and current contract assets arising from transactions accounted for under Topic 606, as follows:

1. Practical expedient. In developing reasonable and supportable forecasts as part of estimating expected credit losses, all entities may elect a practical expedient that assumes that current conditions as of the balance sheet date do not change for the remaining life of the asset.
2. Accounting policy election. An entity other than a public business entity that elects the practical expedient is permitted to make an accounting policy election to consider collection activity after the balance sheet date when estimating expected credit losses.

326-20-30-10A An entity may elect the practical expedient described in paragraphs 326-20-30-10C through 30-10D and an entity other than a public business entity may elect the accounting policy described in paragraphs 326-20-30-10E through 30-10H when developing an estimate of expected credit losses on current accounts receivable and current contract asset balances arising from transactions accounted for under Topic 606 on revenue from contracts with customers. This includes those asset balances acquired in a transaction accounted for under Topic 805 on business combinations or recognized through the consolidation of a variable interest entity that is not a business as described in paragraph 810-10-30-3 that arose from transactions that the acquiree or variable interest entity accounted for under Topic 606.

326-20-30-10F An entity other than a public business entity that applies the practical expedient and the accounting policy election shall estimate its expected credit losses on current accounts receivable and current contract asset balances in the following sequence:

a. The entity shall first consider subsequent collections of those asset balances described in paragraph 326-20-30-10A that were outstanding as of the balance sheet date. No credit loss allowance shall be recorded

BC31. Under current guidance, an entity is required to assess and document its forecast of future economic conditions and the effect of those conditions on estimated expected credit losses as of the balance sheet date. The amendments in this Update provide a practical expedient under which an entity assumes that current conditions as of the balance sheet date do not change for the remaining life of the asset, thereby eliminating the requirement to identify, analyze, and document macroeconomic data as part of developing a reasonable and supportable forecast when estimating expected credit losses.

BC32. Comment letter respondents generally supported the practical expedient. Those respondents explained that the practical expedient is operable and would improve the application of Topic 326 to short-term assets within the scope of the guidance.

BC33. Some comment letter respondents provided feedback that not permitting public business entities to apply the practical expedient could imply that a complex macroeconomic forecast was necessary to estimate expected credit losses for short-term assets within the scope of the amendments in the proposed Update for public business entities. The Board considered that feedback and decided to expand the practical expedient to all entities as discussed in paragraph BC17.

BC34. When applying the practical expedient, an entity is still required to consider other information that affects collectibility such as adjustments to historical loss information to reflect the extent to which current conditions differ from the conditions that existed for the periods over which the historical information was gathered. In applying Topic 326, an entity also is required to reflect customer-specific and company-specific information that is expected to have an effect on the collectibility of outstanding receivables and contract assets.

BC35. For example, if an entity determined that economic conditions as of the balance sheet date differed from the conditions that existed over the period during which historical data were collected because of the onset of a severe economic recession before the balance sheet date, the entity should consider whether an adjustment to historical loss information is necessary. Additionally, an entity that identifies an individual customer that is experiencing financial distress should consider that information in its estimate of expected credit

BC44. The Board decided that an entity should disclose when it has applied the practical expedient and accounting policy election. Most comment letter respondents supported this requirement. Those respondents indicated that it would provide increased transparency, while also facilitating greater comparability and understandability of the estimates of expected credit losses across entities. Comment letter respondents also noted that the disclosure requirement is consistent with required disclosures for other practical expedients and accounting policy elections.

BC45. In addition, the Board decided to require entities other than public business entities that apply the accounting policy election to disclose the date through which collection activity is evaluated after the balance sheet date. Because the Board observed that an entity may change the date through which it evaluates collections under the accounting policy election (as discussed in paragraph BC41), the Board determined that it is important to provide transparency about the date through which the entity is evaluating collection activity when determining its estimate of expected credit losses.

FASB ASC 326 Update.pdf.section_name: Who Is Affected by the Amendments in This Update?
FASB ASC 326 Update.pdf.content:
The amendments in this Update affect entities that apply the practical expedient and accounting policy election (if applicable) when estimating expected credit losses on current accounts receivable and/or current contract assets arising from transactions under Topic 606, including those assets acquired in a transaction accounted for under Topic 805, Business Combinations.

The practical expedient may be applied by all entities, and the accounting policy election may be applied by entities other than public business entities.

BC37. The amendments in this Update permit an entity other than a public business entity that applies the practical expedient to apply an accounting policy election that allows the entity to consider collection activity after the balance sheet date when estimating expected credit losses. If an entity makes this accounting policy election, it will record a credit loss allowance of zero for asset balances within the scope of the amendments as described in paragraph 326-20-30-10A that have been collected as of the date that the financial statements are available to be issued (or the alternative date selected by the entity).

BC38. Comment letter respondents questioned whether entities other than public business entities would be required to update the credit loss rates that would be applied to balances that remain outstanding after an entity has evaluated post-balance-sheet collection activity under the accounting policy election. Specifically, those respondents asked whether the Board intended that the credit loss rates applied in the illustrative Examples used to calculate estimates of expected credit losses should be updated for collection activity after the balance sheet date.

Financial asset

Cash, evidence of an ownership interest in an entity, or a contract that conveys to one entity a right to do either of the following:

Implementation Handbook.pdf.section_name: 2.3.2 Reflect the risk of loss, even when that risk is remote
Implementation Handbook.pdf.content:
2.3.2
Reflect the risk of loss, even when that risk is remote

Excerpt from Accounting Standards Codification
Financial Instruments — Credit Losses — Measured at Amortized Cost

Initial Measurement

Developing an Estimate of Expected Credit Losses

326-20-30-10

An entity's estimate of expected credit losses shall include a measure of the expected risk of credit loss even if that risk is remote, regardless of the method applied to estimate credit losses. However, an entity is not required to measure expected credit losses on a financial asset (or group of financial assets) in which historical credit loss information adjusted for current conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts results in an expectation that nonpayment of the amortized cost basis is zero. Except for the circumstances described in paragraphs 326-20-35-4 through 35-6, an entity shall not expect nonpayment of the amortized cost basis to be zero solely on the basis of the current value of collateral securing the financial asset(s) but, instead, also shall consider the nature of the collateral, potential future changes in collateral values, and historical loss information for financial assets secured with similar collateral.

To accomplish this objective, the entity will create a reasonable and supportable forecast of future economic conditions, as described in ASC 326-20-30-7.

As described further below, at the end of the reasonable and supportable forecast period, the entity cannot estimate a loss of zero. As a result, the entity will be required to revert to historical loss information from the end of the reasonable and supportable forecast period to the end of the contractual life. Reverting to historical information does not imply that the estimate of losses beyond the reasonable and supportable forecast period is also not both reasonable and supportable. Both the forecast and reversion periods are a component of the overall estimate of credit losses and must be supported by management it its entirety.

For receivables with lives of less than one year, changes to economic conditions may not have a significant effect on the estimate of the allowance for expected credit losses because it is less likely that the economic conditions will change significantly enough to influence expected credit losses. However, in more volatile economic environments, it is possible that the estimate could be affected. |

Implementation Handbook.pdf.section_name: 2.5.2 Adjustments to historical loss information
Implementation Handbook.pdf.content:
Adjustments to historical loss information

Excerpt from Accounting Standards Codification
Financial Instruments — Credit Losses — Measured at Amortized Cost

Initial Measurement

Developing an Estimate of Expected Credit Losses

326-20-30-9

An entity shall not rely solely on past events to estimate expected credit losses. When an entity uses historical loss information, it shall consider the need to adjust historical information to reflect the extent to which management expects current conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts to differ from the conditions that existed for the period over which historical information was evaluated. The adjustments to historical loss information may be qualitative in nature and should reflect changes related to relevant data (such as changes in unemployment rates, property values, commodity values, delinquency, or other factors that are associated with credit losses on the financial asset or in the group of financial assets). Some entities may be able to develop reasonable and supportable forecasts over the contractual term of the financial asset or a group of financial assets. However, an entity is not required to develop forecasts over the contractual term of the financial asset or group of financial assets. Rather, for periods beyond which the entity is able to make or obtain reasonable and supportable forecasts of expected credit losses, an entity shall revert to historical loss information determined in accordance with paragraph 326-20-30-8 that is reflective of the contractual term of the financial asset or group of financial assets. An entity shall not adjust historical loss information for existing economic conditions or expectations of future economic conditions for periods that are beyond the reasonable and supportable period. An entity may revert to historical loss information at the input level or based on the entire estimate. An entity may revert to historical loss information immediately, on a straight-line basis, or using another rational and systematic basis.

Implementation Guidance and Illustrations

Implementation Guidance

Information Considered When Estimating Expected Credit Losses

326-20-55-4

Because historical experience may not fully reflect an entity's expectations about the future, management should adjust historical loss information, as necessary, to reflect the current conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts not already reflected in the historical loss information. In making this determination, management should consider characteristics of the financial assets that are relevant in the circumstances. To adjust historical credit loss information for current conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts, an entity should consider significant factors that are relevant to determining the expected collectibility. Examples of factors an entity may consider include any of the following, depending on the nature of the asset (not all of these may be relevant to every situation, and other factors not on the list may be relevant):

a. The borrower's financial condition, credit rating, credit score, asset quality, or business prospects

b. The borrower's ability to make scheduled interest or principal payments

c. The remaining payment terms of the financial asset(s)

d. The remaining time to maturity and the timing and extent of prepayments on the financial asset(s)

e. The nature and volume of the entity's financial asset(s)

f. The volume and severity of past due financial asset(s) and the volume and severity of adversely classified or rated financial asset(s)

Implementation Handbook.pdf.section_name: 2.5.2.1 Adjustments for asset-specific factors and current economic conditions
2.5.2.2 Reasonable and supportable forecasts of future economic conditions
Implementation Handbook.pdf.content:
The standard requires an entity to incorporate reasonable and supportable forecasts of future economic conditions into the estimate of expected credit losses, considering factors that are asset- or borrower-specific and related to expected economic conditions.

Significant judgment is required to develop such a forecast. While entities have experience making forecasts for business and capital planning purposes and for developing fair value estimates, US GAAP provides no guidance on how a forecast of future economic conditions should be developed or how long the forecast period should be.

Most forecasting approaches start with near-term estimates of economic variables, and these estimates affect other variables used in the estimate. Statistical methodologies are then used to determine the path and pace of change for variables over a longer-term horizon. The path and pace of change is influenced by the forecasting party's judgments about future economic conditions. Such statistical methodologies frequently include reversion.

Implementation Handbook.pdf.section_name: Question 2-19: Is an entity required to consider reasonable and supportable forecasts of future economic conditions when estimating the expected lifetime losses on short-term receivables?
Implementation Handbook.pdf.content:
Yes. ASC 326 requires an entity to estimate lifetime expected credit losses considering the entity's forecast of future economic conditions. For receivables with lives of less than one year, changes to economic conditions may not have a significant effect on the estimate of the allowance for expected credit losses because it is less likely that the economic conditions will change significantly enough to influence expected credit losses. However, in more volatile economic environments, it is possible that the estimate could be affected.

However, an entity that elects to apply the practical expedient in ASU 2025-05 may assume the current economic conditions as of the balance sheet date will remain unchanged throughout the forecast period in the development of a reasonable and supportable forecast for current accounts receivable and current contract assets arising from transactions accounted for under ASC 606. Refer to section 2.11.2.2 for more information.

Implementation Handbook.pdf.section_name: How we see it
Implementation Handbook.pdf.content:
How we see it

While the standard requires entities to revert to historical information when they can no longer reliably forecast future economic conditions, we do not expect entities to do this for short-term receivables and contract assets. That is, we generally believe that entities will be able to forecast future economic conditions for the entire contractual life of a short-term receivable and will not need to revert to historical information.

Implementation Handbook.pdf.section_name: 2.11.1 Accounts receivable and other short-term financial assets
Implementation Handbook.pdf.content:
2.11.1 Accounts receivable and other short-term financial assets

Entities are required to measure expected credit losses on short-term financing receivables (e.g., trade accounts receivable). While the methods used to determine the estimate of expected credit losses may differ from the methods used for longer-term financing receivables (e.g., loans), entities still need to consider the asset's contractual life, the risk of loss and reasonable and supportable forecasts of future economic conditions. However, given the short-term nature of these instruments, entities will likely find that adjusting historical losses to reflect their expectation of future conditions involves less measurement uncertainty than for longer-term assets.

The estimate of expected credit losses should reflect the risk of loss, even if management believes no loss has been incurred as of the measurement date. This will likely result in an entity estimating an expected credit loss for most, if not all, receivables, including those listed below, although the amount of the allowance may be insignificant to the financial statements:

• Receivables from borrowers that are current on their payment (i.e., borrowers that are not late payers)

• Individually significant receivables from large customers (e.g., sales to large wholesale customers)

As previously noted, entities can use various methods to measure expected credit losses, such as pooling receivables based on the levels of delinquency (e.g., current, 0–30 days past due, 31–90 days past due, more than 90 days past due) and applying historical loss rates to each pool.

Implementation Handbook.pdf.content:

Financial Instruments — Credit Losses — Measured at Amortized Cost

Initial Measurement

Practical Expedient and Accounting Policy Election for Accounts Receivable and Contract Assets

Pending Content:
Transition Date: (P) December 16, 2025; (N) December 16, 2025 | Transition Guidance: 326-10-65-6
Practical Expedient

326-20-30-10C

For assets described in paragraph 326-20-30-10A, an entity may elect a practical expedient to assume that current conditions as of the balance sheet date do not change for the remaining life of the asset.

326-20-30-10D

When developing an estimate of expected credit losses for assets to which the practical expedient is applied, an entity shall continue to adjust historical loss information to reflect current conditions to the extent that historical loss information does not reflect current conditions. For example, an entity that has identified an individual customer that is experiencing financial distress would consider that information in its estimate of expected credit losses for that customer even if that information has not yet affected its historical loss experience (that is, even if the customer has not defaulted as of the balance sheet date). Similarly, an entity that has expanded its credit policies before the balance sheet date to offer credit to lower-credit-quality customers would consider that information in its estimate of expected credit losses even if that change has not yet affected its historical loss experience (that is, even if the new, lower-credit-quality customers have not defaulted as of the balance sheet date). As another example, if an entity determined that economic conditions as of the balance sheet date were different from the conditions that existed over the period during which historical data were collected because of the onset of a severe economic recession before the balance sheet date, the entity should consider whether an adjustment to historical loss information is necessary. See paragraph 326-20-50-12A for related disclosure requirements and paragraphs 326-20-55-40A through 55-40Q for an illustrative Example.

Implementation Handbook.pdf.section_name: Accounting policy election
Implementation Handbook.pdf.content:
Accounting policy election

Excerpt from Accounting Standards Codification
Financial Instruments — Credit Losses — Measured at Amortized Cost

Initial Measurement

Practical Expedient and Accounting Policy Election for Accounts Receivable and Contract Assets

Pending Content:
Transition Date: (P) December 16, 2025; (N) December 16, 2025 | Transition Guidance: 326-10-65-6

Accounting Policy Election

326-20-30-10E

An entity other than a public business entity that elects the practical expedient in paragraphs 326-20-30-10C through 30-10D may also elect an accounting policy when estimating expected credit losses to consider collection activity after the balance sheet date but before the entity's financial statements are available to be issued (or before any alternative date selected by the entity that is after the balance sheet date but before the financial statements are available to be issued). For example, under this accounting policy election, the allowance for credit losses related to those asset balances described in paragraph 326-20-30-10A that are collected before an entity's financial statements are available to be issued (or before the alternative date selected by the entity) would be zero. See paragraphs 326-20-50-12A through 50-12B for specific disclosure requirements applicable to this accounting policy election.

326-20-30-10F

An entity other than a public business entity that applies the practical expedient and the accounting policy election shall estimate its expected credit losses on current accounts receivable and current contract asset balances in the following sequence:

a. The entity shall first consider subsequent collections of those asset balances described in paragraph 326-20-30-10A that were outstanding as of the balance sheet date. No credit loss allowance shall be recorded for asset balances that have been collected before the financial statements are available to be issued (or before the alternative date selected by the entity).

b. The entity shall then evaluate any remaining uncollected amounts as of the date that the financial statements are available to be issued (or as of the alternative date selected by the entity) using the practical expedient in paragraphs 326-20-30-10C through 30-10D. That evaluation shall be based on the delinquency status of those uncollected balances as of the date that the financial statements are available to be issued (or the alternative date selected by the entity). See paragraphs 326-20-55-40J through 55-40Q for an illustrative Example.

326-20-30-10G

For entities estimating expected credit losses using an aging schedule (as illustrated in paragraphs 326-20-55-37 through 55-40Q), an entity other than a public business entity that elects to consider subsequent collection activity is permitted, but not required, to update historical loss rates for collection activity after the balance sheet date when determining the allowance for credit losses for amounts outstanding as of the balance sheet date that remain uncollected as of the date that the financial statements are available to be issued (or the alternative date selected by the entity).

326-20-30-10H

A change in the date through which an entity considers subsequent collection activity when applying the accounting policy election is not a change in an accounting principle in accordance with Topic 250 on accounting changes and error corrections.

Implementation Handbook.pdf.section_name: 6.3.1.3 Allowance for credit losses and management's estimation process
Implementation Handbook.pdf.content:
Allowance for credit losses and management's estimation process

Excerpt from Accounting Standards Codification
Financial Instruments — Credit Losses — Measured at Amortized Cost

Disclosure

Allowance for Credit Losses

326-20-50-10
An entity shall provide information that enables a financial statement user to do the following:

a. Understand management's method for developing its allowance for credit losses

b. Understand the information that management used in developing its current estimate of expected credit losses

c. Understand the circumstances that caused changes to the allowance for credit losses, thereby affecting the related credit loss expense (or reversal) reported for the period.

326-20-50-11
To meet the objectives in paragraph 326-20-50-10, an entity shall disclose all of the following by portfolio segment and major security type:

a. A description of how expected loss estimates are developed

b. A description of the entity's accounting policies and methodology to estimate the allowance for credit losses, as well as a discussion of the factors that influenced management's current estimate of expected credit losses, including:

1. Past events

2. Current conditions

3. Reasonable and supportable forecasts about the future.

c. A discussion of risk characteristics relevant to each portfolio segment

d. A discussion of the changes in the factors that influenced management's current estimate of expected credit losses and the reasons for those changes (for example, changes in portfolio composition, underwriting practices, and significant events or conditions that affect the current estimate but were not contemplated or relevant during a previous period)

e. Identification of changes to the entity's accounting policies, changes to the methodology from the prior period, its rationale for those changes, and the quantitative effect of those changes

f. Reasons for significant changes in the amount of writeoffs, if applicable

g. A discussion of the reversion method applied for periods beyond the reasonable and supportable forecast period

h. The amount of any significant purchases of financial assets during each reporting period

i. The amount of any significant sales of financial assets or reclassifications of loans held for sale during each reporting period.

Implementation Handbook.pdf.content:
ASC 326-20 includes the following disclosure requirements for past due and nonaccrual assets.

Excerpt from Accounting Standards Codification
Financial Instruments — Credit Losses — Measured at Amortized Cost

Disclosure

Past Due Status

326-20-50-14
To enable a financial statement user to understand the extent of financial assets that are past due, an entity shall provide an aging analysis of the amortized cost basis for financial assets that are past due as of the reporting date, disaggregated by class of financing receivable and major security type. An entity also shall disclose when it considers a financial asset to be past due.

326-20-50-15
The requirements to disclose past-due status in paragraph 326-20-50-14 do not apply to receivables measured at the lower of amortized cost basis or fair value, or trade receivables due in one year or less, except for credit card receivables, that result from revenue transactions within the scope of Topic 605 on revenue recognition or Topic 606 on revenue from contracts with customers.

Nonaccrual Status

326-20-50-16
To enable a financial statement user to understand the credit risk and interest income recognized on financial assets on nonaccrual status, an entity shall disclose all of the following, disaggregated by class of financing receivable and major security type:

a. The amortized cost basis of financial assets on nonaccrual status as of the beginning of the reporting period and the end of the reporting period

b. The amount of interest income recognized during the period on nonaccrual financial assets

c. The amortized cost basis of financial assets that are 90 days or more past due, but are not on nonaccrual status as of the reporting date

d. The amortized cost basis of financial assets on nonaccrual status for which there is no related allowance for credit losses as of the reporting date.

326-20-50-17
An entity's summary of significant accounting policies for financial assets within the scope of this Subtopic shall include all of the following:

a. Nonaccrual policies, including the policies for discontinuing accrual of interest, recording payments received on nonaccrual assets (including the cost recovery method, cash basis method, or some combination of those methods), and resuming accrual of interest, if applicable

b. The policy for determining past-due or delinquency status

c. The policy for recognizing writeoffs within the allowance for credit losses.

326-20-50-18
The requirements to disclose nonaccrual status in paragraphs 326-20-50-16 through 50-17 do not apply to receivables measured at lower of amortized cost basis or fair value, or trade receivables due in one year or less, except for credit card receivables, that result from revenue transactions within the scope of Topic 605 on revenue recognition or Topic 606 on revenue from contracts with customers.

Implementation Handbook.pdf.section_name: 6.3.1.2 Credit quality information (updated July 2024)
Implementation Handbook.pdf.content:
{{EXCERPT_BOX_6312}}
Excerpt from Accounting Standards Codification
Financial Instruments — Credit Losses — Measured at Amortized Cost

Credit Quality Information

Disclosure

326-20-50-4
An entity shall provide information that enables a financial statement user to do both of the following:

a. Understand how management monitors the credit quality of its financial assets

b. Assess the quantitative and qualitative risks arising from the credit quality of its financial assets.

326-20-50-5
To meet the objectives in paragraph 326-20-50-4, an entity shall provide quantitative and qualitative information by class of financing receivable and major security type about the credit quality of financial assets within the scope of this Subtopic (excluding off-balance-sheet credit exposures and repurchase agreements and securities lending agreements within the scope of Topic 860), including all of the following:

a. A description of the credit quality indicator(s)

b. The amortized cost basis, by credit quality indicator

c. For each credit quality indicator, the date or range of dates in which the information was last updated for that credit quality indicator.

326-20-50-8
If an entity discloses internal risk ratings, then the entity shall provide qualitative information on how those internal risk ratings relate to the likelihood of loss.

326-20-50-9
The requirements to disclose credit quality indicators in paragraphs 326-20-50-4 through 50-5 do not apply to receivables measured at the lower of amortized cost basis or fair value, or trade receivables due in one year or less, except for credit card receivables, that result from revenue transactions within the scope of Topic 605 on revenue recognition or Topic 606 on revenue from contracts with customers.

Master Glossary

Credit Quality Indicator

A statistic about the credit quality of a financial asset.
